newsitem.title: GERMANY: Military planners struggle for consensus on Zaire.
newsitem.headline: Military planners struggle for consensus on Zaire.

text.p: Western and African military leaders tried on Saturday to establish how many refugees needed help in Zaire in order to develop military options amid some signs interest in the mission was flagging.

Talks between nations interested in contributing to a mission went on through the day. At an initial meeting on Friday, military planners and aid groups failed to agree on the number of refugees at risk in the region.

"There has still been no decision yet on the number of refugees," said Lieutenant Commander Louis Garneau, a spokesman for the Canadian military delegation at the meeting at the U.S. European Command in Stuttgart.

Support for a planned multi-national task force in east Zaire has cooled with the return of hundreds of thousands of refugees to Rwanda. One European military official at the Stuttgart talks said momentum for the mission had waned.
"The lack of a major U.S. commitment with combat troops is weighing on the minds of people," the official said.
"It seems now as though more people will favour keeping the status quo and not stepping up the commitment since the situation is starting to take care of itself," he said.
It was unclear whether the meeting would end on Saturday night or resume on Sunday, officials said.

Three scenarios in a preliminary discussion document seen by Reuters set out the pros and cons of basing a military relief operation in Rwanda or in Zaire and included a third option of not sending any extra troops at all.

The military meeting took place as the head of the U.N. refugee agency UNHCR appealed in Geneva to the international community to help aid agencies reach hundreds of thousands of Hutu refugees still scattered across eastern Zaire.

Lieutenant-General Maurice Baril of Canada, coordinating the U.N.-authorised mission, told reporters on Friday that estimates presented at the Stuttgart meeting of the number of refugees in need of help varied from 100,000 to 500,000.

After the talks ended on Friday night, Baril denied there was friction between commanders and the aid groups, who have provided higher estimates of the refugee population and have expressed concern that the mission may be scrapped.
"It is not because we have different opinions but that we have different sources of information. They (the aid group representatives) have been away from the refugees for many days," Baril said.
The Stuttgart meeting is expected to consider various military options but leave the final decision of a humanitarian relief mission to individual governments.
A military official at the talks confirmed the paper seen by Reuters was the basis for early discussions by the planners but that significant modifications and additions could be made.

It noted many nations were ready to provide relief from a base in Rwanda, and the option would probably only need light security. But it would require approval from Rwanda, which has so far been reluctant to see an operation on its soil.
Providing relief from a base in Zaire would mean establishing a secure headquarters, probably with heavy forces.
The paper said the idea had support from the Zairean government, but carried a bigger risk of becoming embroiled in regional conflict.
The option would limit efforts to repatriate Hutu refugees who fled from Rwanda in 1994, according to the papers.
It would also need more complex logistical suppport than a Rwanda-based operation, and take more time.
In a third option, external forces would maintain low-level operational help they now give to Rwanda and relief agencies.
